title: 10 Years of Acquired (with Michael Lewis)

Walmart sells a vast number of items, contrasting with Costco's curated approach.

thesis: This episode primarily argues that Costco is Charlie Munger's favorite company, making it a compelling investment case. It contrasts Costco's curated, low-inventory model—which Munger favored—with Walmart's vast assortment approach.

claims.claim: Costco's strategy of selling fewer items creates a curated experience that consumers prefer, avoiding choice paralysis.
claims.quote: In fact, consumers like not having too much choice. There's all this research showing that if you sell 30 different kinds of jams in the supermarket, you will sell less jam than if you sell three kinds of jam. The people just be paralyzed by the choice.

claims.claim: Costco's low inventory turnover and vendor financing model means the business has no working capital other than building more stores.
claims.quote: There's no working capital in this business other than building more Costcos.

claims.claim: Costco's business model relies on a small number of items, allowing merchandisers to deeply understand each product and align incentives.
claims.quote: If you're only going to sell very few things, you're only going to make very few episodes. It puts a lot of onus on making exceptional choices on the things that you do choose to carry.

claims.claim: Costco is Charlie Munger's favorite company, which was a primary reason for the episode.
claims.quote: The only reason we did the episode was it was Charlie Munger's favorite company.

claims.claim: Walmart sells a vast number of items, contrasting with Costco's curated approach.
claims.quote: Unlike Walmart, it has billions of things on the shelf. In Costco, you get what you get. You don't pitch a fit. Whatever's there is there.
